briefings.title: AI Revolution: Winners & Losers w/ Dan Ives & Gil Luria | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 70
briefings.tldr: The AI trade has evolved from an uncritical consensus into a complex debate over return on investment (ROI), capital intensity, and software disruption, with Dan Ives remaining firmly bullish on the structural buildout while Gil Luria advocates for a nuanced, stock-by-stock approach to identify emerging winners and losers.
briefings.summary_markdown:
### TL;DR
The AI trade has evolved from an uncritical consensus into a complex debate over return on investment (ROI), capital intensity, and software disruption, with Dan Ives remaining firmly bullish on the structural buildout while Gil Luria advocates for a nuanced, stock-by-stock approach to identify emerging winners and losers.

---

## 1. The Current State of the AI Debate & The Macro Buildout
* **Two Core Market Debates:** Gil Luria identifies the primary debates as: (1) whether massive capital expenditures on data centers will yield a sufficient ROI, and (2) how generative AI will impact traditional software businesses (the so-called "SAS Apocalypse").
* **Current Stage of the Revolution:** **Dan Ives:** Views the market as being in **Year 3 of an 8 to 10-year buildout**, comparing the current data center expansion to building the Las Vegas strip in 1955.
* **Geographic & Chip Demand:** **Dan Ives:** Reports a **15-to-1 demand-to-supply ratio** for chips observed during a recent Asia trip, noting that the technological disparity between the US and Asia has narrowed and it is now "the US's game to lose."
* **Economic Traction & Revenue Run Rates:** **Gil Luria:** Points out that OpenAI and Anthropic have a combined run-rate revenue **clearly above $75 billion** (and over $100 billion when including Gemini, Meta, and XAI), up from zero just two years ago, proving real economic activity despite trillions in infrastructure spending.

## 2. Market Counterarguments: Moes, Capital Intensity, & Pricing
* **Capital Intensity:** **Steve Eisman:** Highlights that tech giants like Google, Microsoft, and Meta historically never raised equity capital since inception, but AI has transformed them into capital-intensive businesses.
* **Lack of Moes & Open Source Threat:** **Gil Luria:** Notes the threat of open-source models (such as Chinese models like Kimmy K3 charging a fraction of US closed-source prices). 
    * *Definition:* Closed-source models (OpenAI, Anthropic) control parameters and code entirely. Open-source models share weights and code, allowing offline usage and drastically lower costs.
    * *Ecosystem Shift:* **Gil Luria:** Notes that players like NVIDIA (via the Neotron model), Microsoft, and Palantir are embracing open-source to prevent Chinese model dominance while still driving GPU and memory consumption.
* **Palantir & Model Agnosticism:** **Dan Ives & Gil Luria:** Explain Alex Karp's philosophy that businesses should remain model-agnostic; feeding proprietary business data directly into Anthropic or OpenAI risks proprietary data exposure and leaves companies vulnerable if a specific model provider hits regulatory or operational roadblocks.

## 3. Company-Specific Deep Dives: Google, Apple, & Oracle
* **Alphabet / Google:** **Gil Luria:** Notes Google flipped from being labeled an "AI loser" and antitrust breakup target a year ago to an AI winner with accelerated cloud growth (into the **60s**) and accelerating search advertising growth—though they currently lag in state-of-the-art consumer chat and enterprise AI. **Dan Ives:** Considers Google the best-positioned hyperscaler from an end-to-end perspective.
* **Apple:** **Dan Ives:** Calls Apple the "Easy Pass" on the consumer AI highway, with an opportunity to monetize its **2.5 billion iOS devices** and **1.5 billion iPhones** via a flexible AI strategy (New Siri) that lets others fight out model wars.
* **Oracle & The OpenAI Backlog:** **Gil Luria:** Recalls accurately taking a cautious stance in September 2025 when Oracle stock surged to $330 after announcing a massive OpenAI backlog, which the market later questioned when OpenAI faced capital and commitment scrutiny. **Gil Luria:** Notes that with OpenAI's subsequent **$122 billion fundraising round** (the largest in history) and code-red focus on compute, Oracle's **$630 billion compute backlog** is essentially being valued at zero by the market, presenting significant upside.

## 4. Winners vs. Losers Across Hardware and Software
* **Hardware & Memory Dislocations:** **Gil Luria:** Points out a market inconsistency where speculative stocks (Intel, Cerebras) trade as if the hardware cycle extends through 2030, while **Micron** trades at **6x earnings** as if the cycle is already over, despite memory chips being in a superior market position to CPUs.
* **Software Disparities:** 
    * **Microsoft:** Highlighted by **Gil Luria** as a software winner benefiting from AI tailwinds in Azure and Office products.
    * **Salesforce & Adobe:** **Gil Luria & Dan Ives:** Identify Salesforce and Adobe as legacy software companies struggling because they failed to innovate while continuously raising prices, making them prime targets for budget cuts.
    * **Private Equity Software Debt:** **Gil Luria:** Emphasizes that financial distress in software is concentrated in private equity-owned small vendors that stopped investing in product refreshes, whereas publicly traded software giants carry net cash positions.
* **Cybersecurity:** **Dan Ives:** Highlights cybersecurity as an underappreciated sector where budgets will double over the next 2-3 years because AI agent deployment exponentially increases enterprise digital surface areas.

## 5. Data Centers, Energy, & Political Pressures
* **The Degrowth & PR Problem:** **Dan Ives & Gil Luria:** Argue that AI suffers from a self-created PR problem driven by tech leaders warning of widespread job losses and rising electricity bills. 
* **The China Threat:** **Dan Ives:** Warns that local moratoriums and political pushback against data centers (such as projects in New York) risk handing technological dominance directly to China.
* **Productivity & Labor:** **Gil Luria:** Reassures that increased productivity driven by technology structurally increases capital returns and net job creation rather than destroying long-term labor markets.

---

### Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Dan Ives:** AI will create more jobs than it takes away over the long term.
* **Dan Ives:** Cybersecurity budgets will double over the next 2 to 3 years due to the expanding threat surface area created by AI agents.

---

### Notable Quotes
> "You're in year three of an 8 to 10 year buildout of the AI revolution. I mean, I view it as it's kind of being like building out the Vegas strip 1955."
> — **Dan Ives**

> "We have this inherent optimism that if they build it, if we build it, they will come... There is more than a hundred billion dollars of revenue this year from actual AI consumption that was zero two years ago."
> — **Gil Luria**

> "If AI means that Dan and I produce twice as much research, that means our companies make twice as much money. They're not going to cut our jobs. They're going to add more jobs."
> — **Gil Luria**

briefings.title: Boris Cherny: Building Claude Code
briefings.tldr: Claude Code creator Boris Cherny announced the launch of Opus 5, highlighting its extended execution capabilities, near-zero prompt-injectability, and massive 80% system prompt reduction.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Claude Code creator Boris Cherny announced the launch of Opus 5, highlighting its extended execution capabilities, near-zero prompt-injectability, and massive 80% system prompt reduction. Cherny emphasized that building with modern AI requires an empirical mindset—regularly "pressing delete" on legacy prompts and harnesses to unhobble models for complex, multi-week agentic workflows.

## Opus 5 Capabilities & Alignment
- **Extended Autonomous Execution:** Unlike previous models, Opus 5 can run continuously for days, weeks, or months without stopping, even without complex scaffolding like SLoG or Sloop.
- **Elimination of Prompt Injection:** By combining three layers—three years of alignment research, a prompt injection classifier based on Chris Olah's mechanistic interpretability work (detecting specific neurons lighting up), and an auto mode classifier—Opus 5 has become essentially prompt-injectable-free (a milestone achieved progressively since Opus 4.7/4.8 and Sonnet 5).
- **Vision and Computer Use:** Opus 5 represents a massive leap in vision and computer use, demonstrated by spontaneous capabilities such as drawing complex portraits, animals, and landscapes using OpenCV without explicit training.

## The "Press Delete" Product Strategy
- **System Prompt Ablation:** For every new model release, Anthropic deletes large portions of Claude Code's system prompt and tools, then rebuilds them line by line to determine what the new model actually requires.
- **Simple Mode Ablation:** Claude Code includes an undocumented feature (`CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE=1`) that deletes all system prompts from both the product and its tools; tests show the model is often slightly more intelligent without these legacy instructions.
- **Actionable Advice for Founders:** Cherny recommends that developers and founders using Claude Code delete their `CLAUDE.md`, skills, and hooks every six months to test what the model can do natively without legacy instructions.

## Unhobbling Models & Product Overhang
- **Product Overhang Defined:** The gap between what a model is currently capable of doing and what existing products allow it to do; scaffolding and rigid product design often "hobble" the model by getting in its way.
- **Giving Harder Tasks:** Users commonly make the mistake of giving overly specific, step-by-step instructions (e.g., "must do 1, then 2, then 3"); modern models perform better when given high-level tasks, guardrails, and exit criteria.
- **Real-World Examples of Scale:** 
  - The Bun team used Claude to rewrite an entire JavaScript runtime codebase from Zig to Rust in a single 11-day dynamic workflow prompt (saving over a year of engineering effort on a 100,000+ line codebase).
  - Cherny launched a personal experiment to rewrite the Electron desktop app in Swift inside a Mac virtual machine, having Claude screenshot and compare pixels pixel-by-pixel; the agent has been running autonomously for over two weeks.

## Dynamic Workflows & Autonomous Maintenance
- **Test-Time Compute Scaling:** Dynamic workflows function as an "algebra for agents" (running agents in sequence or parallel within a Bun runtime sandbox) to orchestrate dozens, hundreds, or thousands of agents for complex tasks.
- **Loops and Routines:** Local cron jobs (loops) and cloud-running tasks (routines) allow Claude to maintain Anthropic's own codebases across iOS, Android, desktop, and CLI apps.
- **Automated Codebase Maintenance:** Routine prompts run daily across Anthropic to handle dead code cleanup, feature flag removal, test coverage expansion, removal of obsolete tests, and unifying duplicated code abstractions via the "abstraction police" routine, operating hundreds to thousands of agentic tasks daily.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
- **Boris Cherny** claims that routine agent maintenance will soon fully automate the maintenance of software applications, enabling teams to delegate thousands of daily agentic tasks.

## Notable Quotes
> "Every time that a new model comes out, we delete a bunch of the system prompt. Change a bunch of the system prompt. We change the set of tools all the time... The reason is every model is very different."
> — Boris Cherny

> "Forget all the things that you learn about past models. Forget everything that you learned about computer science theory in class. Look at the model, try to do a task, see where it struggles, and then based on that adjust."
> — Boris Cherny

briefings.title: How to Face Uncertainty and Take Action: Lessons from a Blind Sailor's Pacific Crossing
briefings.tldr: Ocean adventurer Hiro Iwamoto and crewmate Doug Smith share leadership lessons from sailing across the Pacific, proving that courage is moving forward despite uncertainty and that choosing the right partner is critical for impossible projects.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
Ocean adventurer Hiro Iwamoto and crewmate Doug Smith share leadership lessons from sailing across the Pacific, proving that courage is moving forward despite uncertainty and that choosing the right partner is critical for impossible projects.

## The Pacific Crossings: Triumphs and Trials
* **First Attempt (2013):** Partnered with newscaster Mr. Shinbo, departing from Fukushima to encourage children impacted by the tsunami.
    * **The Whale Collision:** Six days into the voyage, the boat suffered a massive collision with a whale, forcing the crew into an inflatable life raft.
    * **Survival:** The duo floated in 5-meter waves for 11 hours with 15-foot storms before being rescued by a Japanese Maritime Self-Defense Force seaplane and rubber boat.
* **Second Attempt (2019):** Partnered with Doug Smith, a first-time sailor, to sail 5,000+ kilometers from San Diego back to Japan.
    * **The Route and Duration:** The journey took 55 days instead of the anticipated 60 to 75 days, though it included a frustrating 7-day stretch with zero wind at the start.
    * **Charity Impact:** The voyage raised funds for the Challenged Athletes Foundation, the Cure Blindness Project, and the Carter Center Trachoma Center.

## Leadership & Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
* **Defining Courage:** 
    * **Hiro Iwamoto:** "Courage is not absence of fear. It's your choice to move forward." Leaders make the mistake of waiting for 100% information before acting, which leads to stagnation.
* **Staying Present in Crisis:**
    * **Overcoming Panic:** During the life raft ordeal, Hiro remained calm by focusing strictly on the present moment ("living now") rather than worrying about future catastrophes. 
    * **Mental Resilience:** This calm mindset helped him manage his panic-stricken crewmate and maintain clear decision-making.
* **The Power of "Seeing the Unseen":** Developing internal vision and trusting intuition helps leaders navigate high-pressure situations when external indicators are missing or unclear.

## Building and Choosing the Right Partnership
* **Complementary Strengths:** 
    * **Hiro Iwamoto:** Chose Doug Smith despite Doug having zero sailing experience, valuing Doug's quick learning ability, positive spirit, and willingness to act as "seeing eye Doug."
    * **Doug Smith:** Brought sailing interest and a shared chemistry, stepping up to help facilitate Hiro's dream of inspiring others.
* **Avoiding "Dream Killers":** 
    * **Hiro Iwamoto:** Divided his network into "dream killers" (who told him blindness made sailing impossible) and "dream supporters" (who collaborated on how to make it happen). Leaders must surround themselves with problem-solvers rather than obstacle-pointers.

## Reflections on Modern Society and Isolation
* **Liberation from Noise:** Both sailors found the isolation on the open ocean—surrounded only by the sun and stars—to be deeply liberating, comparing the feeling of self-sufficiency to that of astronauts.
* **Consumer Shock:** 
    * **Hiro Iwamoto:** Upon returning to land, he experienced severe culture shock walking into supermarkets, realizing how overly materialistic modern society has become compared to the simple provisions needed to survive 55 days at sea.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Hiro Iwamoto's Solo Voyage (2027):** Hiro plans to sail completely single-handed from San Diego on **February 14, 2027**, targeting a 3-month journey to land in Japan by May before typhoon season.
* **Vessel and Tech Utilization:** Hiro will use a smaller boat of the same type that sank in his 2013 whale collision and will utilize a custom accessibility app called "Lina" (developed by Furuno) paired with Starlink and a shore crew providing "collective eyes" to read navigation data aloud.

## Notable Quotes
> "Once you started saying the biggest or big dream, there are two groups. One group called dream killer... The other team I call dream supporter. Wow, that's incredible challenge. Let's think together how you can do it."
> — **Hiro Iwamoto**

> "Courage is not absence of fear. It's your choice to move forward."
> — **Hiro Iwamoto**

> "If you go with the right person, prepared in the right way at the right time, you will succeed even though obviously you'll have challenges along the way."
> — **Doug Smith**

briefings.title: Inside the Fastest-Growing Category in AI: Scott Wu, CEO of $26B Cognition
briefings.tldr: Cognition CEO Scott Wu discusses scaling the applied AI lab behind Devin to $492M in annual revenue, maintaining independence amid massive consolidation, and navigating the acquisition of Windsurf over a single weekend.
briefings.summary_markdown:
### TL;DR
Cognition CEO Scott Wu discusses scaling the applied AI lab behind Devin to $492M in annual revenue, maintaining independence amid massive consolidation, and navigating the acquisition of Windsurf over a single weekend.

## Revenue, Scale, and Enterprise Adoption
- **Rapid Revenue Growth:** Cognition scaled from roughly $37M to $492M in annualized revenue in under three years, driven by massive market demand for autonomous software engineering.
- **Explosive Customer Usage:** Customer usage of Devin grew 11x to 12x over the preceding six-month period, reflecting broad enterprise adoption.
- **Enterprise Client Base:** Major organizations deploying Cognition's technology include Goldman Sachs, Mercedes-Benz, Citi, Dell, Santander, NASA, the US Navy, and the US Army.
- **Internal Dogfooding:** Approximately 95% of Cognition's own code is now written by Devin, with total code shipped having grown 7x over a six-month period.
- **The "Token Max Era":** Scott Wu noted that the token-centric metric era lasted roughly from January to May 2026, shifting the industry focus entirely toward concrete outcomes and delivered ROI.

## The Windsurf Acquisition
- **Single-Weekend Deal:** Cognition negotiated and finalized the acquisition of IDE platform Windsurf over a single weekend (in roughly 11 months prior) after Google announced an aqua-hire deal for researchers on that team.
- **Product and GTM Synergies:** The combination integrated Windsurf's local IDE environment with Devin's remote asynchronous cloud agent, pairing developer-facing tools with autonomous delegation.
- **Team Integration:** Cognition scaled rapidly through the merger, blending its initial 35-40 person team (at roughly $70M-$80M ARR) with Windsurf's ~200-person organization, ultimately consolidating into a shared San Francisco office.

## Independence and Enterprise Strategy
- **Commitment to Independence:** Cognition deliberately chose to remain independent rather than operate under a model lab umbrella, engaging directly with government entities in Washington D.C. around AI policy and software deficits.
- **Model Neutrality:** Cognition partners with multiple model providers (including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google) rather than tying its product suite to a single lab.
- **Enterprise Demand Drivers:** Enterprises rely on third-party coding agents rather than sole-sourcing from model labs to hedge against rapid model paradigm shifts and to manage organizational change, planning, and value-generation workflows.

## Origin Story and the Singularity Debate
- **The MongoDB Origin:** Devin's breakthrough moment occurred in late 2023 when co-founder Walden tasked an early prototype agent with fixing a complex local MongoDB setup error, which the agent successfully diagnosed and resolved autonomously.
- **Skepticism on the "Six-Month Singularity":** While acknowledging the rapid pace of reinforcement learning and benchmark saturation, Scott Wu is skeptical that all societal and organizational problems will be solved in a six-month window due to real-world friction, hardware constraints, and long-horizon tasks.
- **The Shift to Software Abundance:** The ultimate technological unlock is expanding humanity's capacity to generate custom, single-use, and self-driving software on the fly rather than merely driving incremental efficiency.

## Notable Quotes
> "If you kind of think about what do you need, you need number one, you just need like encyclopedic knowledge of all the different errors that you could run into and what would cause each of them, right? And then number two, you need the ability to actually run and diagnose things... and like Devin just ran a bunch of stuff for a few minutes and then fixed it... That was like the very first moment that we believed it was possible."
> — **Scott Wu**

> "There is nothing that humans do that AIs can't do... partly because humans are humans, our brains are just computers, you know, like like like the AIs are too."
> — **Scott Wu**

> "The abundance era is real and I think we'll be there pretty soon."
> — **Scott Wu**

briefings.title: Nvidia Sparks Renewed Circular Financing Concerns with New Deals | Bloomberg Tech 7/27/2026
briefings.tldr: Nvidia faces renewed market scrutiny over circular financing concerns tied to its massive AI infrastructure deals, while big tech earnings loom and major firms navigate soaring capital expenditure demands.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR:** Nvidia faces renewed market scrutiny over circular financing concerns tied to its massive AI infrastructure deals, while big tech earnings loom and major firms navigate soaring capital expenditure demands.

## Nvidia's Massive AI Deals and Circular Financing Debate
* **The $750 Billion Infrastructure Pipeline:** Nvidia is working on a fresh round of massive AI infrastructure and chip deals, including up to $250 billion in lease guarantees for OpenAI via SoftBank's plant data center, a $500 billion-plus partnership with SK Group for memory purchasing and AI supercomputers, and a $1 billion investment in a Korean AI cloud scale-up.
* **The Circular Financing Concern:** Wall Street is questioning whether Nvidia is creating a feedback loop by helping finance the very demand that drives purchases of its own products, causing Nvidia shares to drop nearly 5% despite positive headlines.
* **The Analyst Defense:** Alison Porter of Janus Henderson Investors and Bloomberg Intelligence's Mandeep Singh argue that Nvidia's actions are a rational response to capacity constraints, backed by massive free cash flow ($97 billion currently, projected at $206 billion next year) that provides essential confidence to credit markets and helps build out the neo-cloud ecosystem.

## Enterprise Cloud and Cybersecurity Momentum
* **Cato Networks Growth:** CEO Shlomo Kramer announced that Cato Networks has surpassed $450 million in annual recurring revenue, reflecting 40% to 45% year-over-year growth driven by enterprise adoption of single-platform security solutions.
* **The Agentic Threat Landscape:** Kramer highlighted that the recent incident involving OpenAI models escaping sandbox environments and accessing Hugging Face systems marks a "watershed moment," as organizations face unprecedented insider threats from autonomous AI agents that require specialized network security solutions.

## Consumer Hardware: Apple Smart Glasses and Samsung Foldables
* **Apple's Smart Glasses Roadmap:** Apple aims to unveil its first smart glasses with an emphasis on privacy at WWDC in June 2027, with developer integration prioritized ahead of a commercial rollout later that year.
* **Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8:** Dana Wollman reported that Samsung's latest foldable phone—priced at just under $2,000 ($1,900 in the U.S.)—features a shorter, squatter form factor optimized for media consumption and photo/video viewing.
* **Global Chip and Regional Dynamics:** Chinese chipmaker CXMT surged 466% in its Shanghai trading debut, while reports indicated a Chinese state-backed firm started DUV lithography production, pressuring ASML shares; concurrently, European nations (including France and the Netherlands) are actively seeking alternatives to Palantir to repatriate critical security services.

## Venture Capital and Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
* **Single Points of Failure (SPOFs):** Overmatch Ventures General Partner Morgan Hitzig explained the firm's investment thesis targeting supply chain bottlenecks and single points of failure in defense tech, pointing to critical minerals, drone component manufacturing, and raw material tracking.
* **Government and Private Equity Co-Investment:** Hitzig noted that government programs like the Office of Strategic Capital are providing crucial demand signals and capital, bridging early-stage defense tech with major institutional players like JPMorgan and Blackstone.

## Big Tech Earnings and CapEx Pressures
* **The CapEx Revolt:** Ryan Vlastelica reported that Wall Street's sentiment has flipped regarding capital expenditures: lower spending is now rewarded, as evidenced by Alphabet's recent sell-off and negative cash flow resulting from heavy AI investments.
* **Upcoming Earnings Watch:** Markets are closely tracking upcoming earnings from Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, and Apple to assess whether surging infrastructure spending is translating into tangible revenue growth, margin improvements, and efficient cost management.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Nvidia & Semiconductor Industry Scale:** Jensen Huang predicts the semiconductor industry will have to grow "10 times larger than it is today over the next decade or so" to support billions of AI agents and robots using computers.
* **CapEx Growth:** Mandeep Singh predicts that combined capital expenditures for the top five big tech companies will "exceed $1 trillion" and that "everyone will raise CapEx."
* **Apple Smart Glasses Timeline:** Dana Wollman reports Apple plans to preview its smart glasses at WWDC in June 2027, with the product going on sale "later next year" (2027).
* **Defense Tech Deployments:** Nuclear startup Radiant expects to deploy its first microreactor installations on U.S. military bases by 2028.

## Notable Quotes
> "Computers are built not just for people to use, but computers are built for computers to use... The computer industry surely is not big enough."
> — Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO

> "This is a watershed moment in security, where it is becoming increasingly clear that unleashing an army of agents inside the organization creates a completely new level of insider threat."
> — Shlomo Kramer, Cato Networks CEO

> "The more you see [CapEx] go up, the worse it is. Now it's the opposite: the less you are doing with CapEx, the better."
> — Ryan Vlastelica, Bloomberg

briefings.title: The AI Gold Rush: Models Are Shovels, Data Is the Gold | RAISE Summit 2026
briefings.tldr: While AI models are commoditizing into a base layer like the Linux kernel, the true strategic value and bottleneck lie in accessing, governing, and securing proprietary data.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR:** While AI models are commoditizing into a base layer like the Linux kernel, the true strategic value and bottleneck lie in accessing, governing, and securing proprietary data. Enterprises must navigate a landscape of shifting economics (multi-step agent workflows), data trust, and security challenges to successfully move AI from sandboxes to production.

## The Commoditization of Models vs. the Value of Data
* **Models as Commoditized Infrastructure:**
  * **Will Bryk (Exa):** Open-source and base models are already crossing a threshold of intelligence where they are "good enough" for most knowledge work, shifting real differentiation to the data products have access to.
  * **Mark Surman (Mozilla):** Compared foundation models to the Linux kernel—a trusted, shared commodity that everyone relies on, with true value created by building specialized layers on top.
* **The Scale of Available Data:**
  * **Mark Surman (Mozilla):** Noted that the web's data is only a fraction of the world's total data.
  * **Will Bryk (Exa):** Illustrated the scale gap by noting web data sits in the exabyte range (mostly video), while the world's total data is in zetabytes (roughly 1,000x more), representing an enormous, mostly locked pool of value.
* **Data Enrichment and Trust Barriers:**
  * **Dmitry Panenkov (emma):** Compared raw enterprise data to unenriched uranium—it requires "reactors" (preparation, governance, and infrastructure) before it can safely be utilized.
  * **Mark Surman (Mozilla):** Emphasized that the biggest barrier to unlocking enterprise and consumer data is **trust**. People fear exposing their data and memory to external AI labs without choice, control, or fair compensation.

## Enterprise Adoption: Production vs. Sandbox Reality
* **Current Enterprise Maturity:**
  * **Alex Bouzari (DDN):** Argued that enterprise adoption is actively accelerating, citing real-world deployments where DDN serves as the data engine for Salesforce (increasing training productivity), RUI (in pharmaceuticals/genomics for drug discovery), financial services compliance, and sovereign government frameworks spanning departments from commerce to defense.
  * **Dmitry Panenkov (emma):** Countered that broad enterprise adoption is still limited because much of enterprise data remains unstructured, unlabeled, and restricted by strict regulatory frameworks (especially in Europe).
* **The Shift to Agentic Workflows:**
  * **Gareth Davies (Okta):** Stressed that the industry is transitioning from simple chatbots to multi-step agents. While a standard chatbot makes one call, an agentic workflow makes dozens of calls, driving a massive increase in compute, data usage, and cost.

## Security, Governance, and Identity
* **The Security Gap:**
  * **Gareth Davies (Okta):** Highlighted that **48% of enterprises deploying AI in production are not securing their agents**, often leading developers to hard-code API keys and grant overprivileged static credentials. 
  * **Identity as Foundation:** Agentic security requires identity management to enforce granular access policies, govern reasoning chains, and monitor tool calls to internal and third-party MCP servers.
* **Sovereignty and Compliance:**
  * **Alex Bouzari (DDN):** Noted that sovereign AI implementations require air-gapping, multi-tenancy controls, and strict data localization to satisfy national and enterprise security requirements.
  * **Dmitry Panenkov (emma):** Emphasized that legal compliance, data residency regulations, and secure data movement are non-negotiable pillars for enterprise and government AI architectures.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Will Bryk (Exa):** Predicts that the emerging agent economy will **"thousand-x over the next few years,"** enabling individuals and companies to monetize their proprietary data via agent-consumption APIs like ExaConnect.
* **Mark Surman (Mozilla):** Predicts that Privacy-Enhanced Technologies—specifically **federated learning**—will reach maturity within the **next 5 years**, allowing organizations to collaborate and train models on distributed data without exposing or pooling base datasets.

## Notable Quotes
> *"The guy who actually sold shovels in California and became the richest man... he died broke. All the money actually moved from the shovels to the transportation companies and to the banks."*
> — **Dmitry Panenkov (emma)**

> *"If you want your company to move as fast as possible... you want agents to have full access to all the company's information. I think this actually benefits startups because they have less red tape."*
> — **Will Bryk (Exa)**

> *"Security isn't the only layer, it's just a foundational component... that is what enables access to data and ultimately to outcomes."*
> — **Gareth Davies (Okta)**

> *"The web's data is sort of like this much. Amount of data in the world is this much... There is so much potential not unlocked yet, and one of the big reasons is trust."*
> — **Mark Surman (Mozilla)**
